A host process uses the machine's normal filesystem and process environment directly.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Containerized deployment packages a Go binary with a defined filesystem and process configuration as an image. Direct deployment copies or builds the binary on a host and relies more heavily on that host's installed files and service manager.

A container process still runs on the host kernel but receives isolated namespaces, resource controls, image layers, and explicit mounts and networks. A host process uses the machine's normal filesystem and process environment directly.

For example, the same `catalog-api@sha256:...` image can be tested and promoted, while configuration changes at runtime. A direct release might copy `catalog-api` to a server and let systemd manage its user, environment file, restart, and logs.

The right unit is the whole operating model: number of services, deployment frequency, platform skills, rollback needs, isolation, and cost. Adding Kubernetes to one rarely changed binary can create more work than value.

Containers fit teams that want the same artifact in CI and deployment, image-based rollbacks, or an orchestrated service platform. Direct binaries remain an excellent choice for simple services where a host service manager and a small release process meet the requirement.

sections.title: The core model: containerized Go deployment
sections.content:
containerized Go deployment is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

A Go executable is already a strong deployment unit, which makes the container decision more nuanced than it is for runtimes with large host dependencies. An image adds a filesystem snapshot, metadata, distribution through a registry, and a standard contract for container platforms. Direct deployment can provide equally reliable restarts, users, environment files, and logs through a service manager, with less tooling. Containers become especially valuable when many services share one delivery platform or when immutable artifacts and automated rollouts are established practices. They also add responsibilities: base images need updates, registries and provenance matter, container networking differs from host networking, and state must live outside replaceable layers. Security comes from several controls together—minimal contents, non-root execution, capabilities, read-only paths, resource limits, and host hardening—not from the word container. The decision should reduce total delivery and operating risk rather than follow a trend.

sections.title: containerized Go deployment example
sections.content:
~~~text
Direct:    source -> go build -> binary -> service manager -> host process
Container: source -> image build -> registry -> container runtime -> host process
~~~

sections.title: containerized Go deployment at a glance
sections.content:
| Concern | Container image | Direct binary |
|---|---|---|
| Artifact | Binary plus runtime filesystem/config | Binary plus release files |
| Isolation | Namespaces and resource controls | Host user/process controls |
| Distribution | Registry and digest | Package, object store, or copy |
| Operations | Runtime or orchestrator | Service manager and host tooling |
